subject: biochemistry
title: Glycosaminoglycans, proteoglycans and the mucopolysaccharidoses: Hurler and Hunter syndromes

steps.tx: Glycosaminoglycans are unbranched heteropolysaccharide **chains** composed of repeating disaccharide units: an amino sugar (glucosamine or galactosamine) and an acidic uronic acid (glucuronic acid or iduronic acid). Due to abundant sulfate and carboxyl groups, glycosaminoglycans carry dense negative charges that attract sodium ions and water molecules, creating hydrated gel matrices capable of resisting massive mechanical compressive forces in articular cartilage.
steps.say: Glycosaminoglycans are unbranched polysaccharide chains of repeating amino sugars and uronic acids. Heavily sulfated and carboxylated, they carry dense negative charges that bind water, forming hydrated gel cushions that absorb mechanical compression in cartilage and joints.

rows: Synovial fluid, vitreous humor, umbilical cord (non-sulfated)
Cartilage, bone, heart valves (most abundant GAG)

steps.tx: Proteoglycan monomers consist of multiple glycosaminoglycan chains covalently attached to a core **protein** through a specific trisaccharide-serine linker (xylose-galactose-galactose). In articular cartilage, hundreds of aggrecan monomers non-covalently associate with a central hyaluronic acid filament via link proteins, creating colossal supramolecular proteoglycan aggregates with molecular weights exceeding millions of Daltons, essential for joint lubrication and shock absorption.
steps.say: Proteoglycans consist of glycosaminoglycan chains attached to a core protein through a xylose-galactose-galactose linker. In cartilage, aggrecan monomers bind hyaluronic acid backbones via link proteins, forming giant supramolecular aggregates that provide joint elasticity and lubrication.

steps.tx: The image shows feathery red bristles radiating from central stalks tied to a long blue filament. Each bristle is an **aggrecan** monomer built on a **core protein** carrying sulfated chains. Many monomers anchor to one **hyaluronic acid** backbone through link protein, forming a giant water holding aggregate that cushions cartilage in joints.
steps.say: The picture shows many brush like aggrecan monomers fixed to a central hyaluronic acid thread by link protein. Each monomer has a core protein with many chondroitin sulfate chains fanning out. The negative charges hold water and resist compression. This shape explains shock absorption in cartilage.

vis.alt: Blue filament backbone holds many brush like aggrecan monomers with core protein and chondroitin sulfate chains.
vis.caption: Aggrecan monomers on hyaluronic backbone Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Degradation of glycosaminoglycans occurs inside lysosomes via sequential cleavage by acid **hydrolases**. Inherited deficiencies in specific lysosomal enzymes result in the mucopolysaccharidoses, characterized by progressive intracellular accumulation of undegraded dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate. Cells become distended with storage vacuoles, leading to coarse facial features, skeletal dysostosis multiplex, hepatosplenomegaly, valvular heart disease, and progressive neurocognitive decline.
steps.say: Glycosaminoglycans are broken down in lysosomes by sequential acid hydrolases. Genetic deficiencies cause mucopolysaccharidoses, where undegraded dermatan and heparan sulfate accumulate. This causes coarse facial features, skeletal dysostosis multiplex, organomegaly, and neurological decline.

left.title: Hurler syndrome (MPS I)
points: Severe intellectual disability and early death

right.title: Hunter syndrome (MPS II)
points: Aggressive behavioral changes and retinal degeneration

steps.tx: The films show broad oar shaped ribs and beaked front edges of vertebrae. These are classic **dysostosis multiplex** changes of the **mucopolysaccharidoses**, where failed **lysosomal breakdown** leaves dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate stored in bone and cartilage. Spot beaked vertebrae and paddle ribs to pick a storage disorder in a child with coarse features.
steps.say: The chest views label wide oar shaped ribs. The spine view labels anterior beaking of vertebrae. Both reflect poor bone modeling when storage material fills cells. In a child with coarse face and stiff joints, these films favor a mucopolysaccharidosis over simple rickets.

vis.alt: Paired chest films show oar shaped ribs and anteriorly beaked vertebrae with labels.
vis.caption: Oar ribs and beaked vertebrae in storage disease Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Sanfilippo syndrome represents **mucopolysaccharidosis** type III, caused by impaired catabolism of heparan sulfate alone. In contrast to Hurler syndrome, children with Sanfilippo syndrome exhibit relatively mild somatic manifestations and minimal dysostosis multiplex. However, accumulation of heparan sulfate within the central nervous system triggers severe, devastating neurodegeneration, profound sleep cycle disruption, intractable behavioral hyperactivity, and eventual loss of motor and language milestones.
steps.say: Sanfilippo syndrome, MPS type III, involves selective failure of heparan sulfate breakdown. Unlike Hurler syndrome, skeletal and facial changes are mild. However, heparan sulfate accumulation in the brain causes severe behavioral hyperactivity, sleep disturbances, dementia, and fatal neurodegeneration.

rows: Severe progressive childhood dementia, mild somatic signs
Severe skeletal dysplasia, odontoid hypoplasia, normal intellect
